column2: Every part has a drawing or model
column3: Does each line on the RFQ have a drawing, a model or both, and do the part numbers on them match the RFQ?
column4: A line quoted from a description alone is a guess; a drawing that carries another part number means one part was never sent.

column3: Which revision is each drawing, does it match the revision the RFQ asks for, and is the model the same revision as the drawing?
column4: The price is for the revision quoted. A model at Rev C with a drawing at Rev B is two different parts until the buyer says which one governs.

column3: If the drawing and the model disagree, which one does the customer say governs, and are there dimensions only on the drawing?
column4: Many shops program from the model and inspect to the drawing; a note saying which governs settles the argument before the first article, not after.

column3: Do you have every specification the drawing calls out (material, finish, heat treat, welding, inspection), at the revision it names?
column4: A callout you have not read can add a process, a test or a certification you did not price.

column3: Is the material fully specified (alloy, temper or condition, form), can you buy it at the size you need, and is a substitute allowed?
column4: “Aluminum” is not a material; 6061-T6 plate and 7075-T651 bar price and machine differently, and an unavailable size changes the blank.

column3: Which features carry the tightest tolerances or GD&T callouts, and can your machines hold and your gauges measure them?
column4: One tight bore can decide the machine, the setup count and the inspection time for the whole part.

column3: What surface roughness is called out, where, and what edge break or deburr note applies?
column4: A fine finish on a sealing face may need a finishing pass or a grind; “break all edges” on a part with many edges is real minutes.

column3: Which threads, thread classes and hole depths are called out, and do any need special tools or gauges?
column4: Deep holes, small taps and thread gauges you do not own add time and tooling cost.

column3: Which outside processes are called out (anodize, plating, passivation, paint, heat treat), to which specification, and who supplies them?
column4: Outside processes have lot minimums and lead times of their own, and a masking note can cost more than the coating.

column3: Does the part need part marking, serial numbers, bagging, special packaging or labels?
column4: Small per-part steps add up over a lot and are easy to forget at the quoting stage.

column3: Which quantities does the buyer want prices for, is it a one-off, a blanket order or scheduled releases, and is there a prototype lot first?
column4: Setup and lot minimums spread differently at each quantity; a blanket order with releases is priced and stocked differently from one lot.

column3: When does the buyer need the parts, when must the quote be in, and can you deliver with what is already on the floor?
column4: A price you cannot deliver on loses the customer more surely than a high price.

column3: Have you quoted or made this part number before, at which revision and price, and did that quote win?
column4: Last time's price, time and problems are the best estimate you have, and a buyer notices when the same part is priced differently.

column3: Does the buyer want material certifications, a certificate of conformance or process certs from your finishers?
column4: Certs have to be ordered with the material and kept; a mill cert requested after the material arrives may not be available.

column3: Is a first-article inspection required (for aerospace work, often to AS9102), a CMM report, a sampling plan or 100% inspection?
column4: A full first-article report on a complex part can take longer than machining the first part, and it is often unpriced.

column3: Does the purchase order or the buyer's supplier manual require a quality system registered to ISO 9001 or AS9100, or other quality clauses?
column4: Quality clauses on the PO bind you once you accept it; read them at the quote, not when the order arrives.

column3: Is the drawing marked ITAR or EAR, or as Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), and can your shop lawfully receive and store it?
column4: Export-controlled and CUI drawings have handling rules of their own; ask someone qualified before you open them, not after.

column3: Is it a defense or government job, and which clauses flow down to you (for example DFARS 252.204-7012 on safeguarding covered defense information, or 252.225-7009 on specialty metals)?
column4: Flowdowns can restrict where material comes from and how you store the drawings; a clause you cannot meet means no-quote.

column3: Does the customer supply the material or parts, and who pays when one scraps?
column4: Free-issue material changes the price and the risk; settle the scrap terms on the quote.

column3: Are the buyer's payment terms and shipping terms (FOB point, who pays freight) ones you accept?
column4: Net 90 on a large material buy is a loan to the customer; know it before you price.

column3: After all of the above: do you want this job at a price the buyer is likely to pay, and if not, have you told them so?
column4: A prompt no-quote keeps the buyer's goodwill and your estimator's time for the work you want.
